title: Do good and throw it in the sea
goal: In Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Sēf there, he hears you helped your neighbour; play it down, and understand his proverb
tip: Learn a proverb whole, for recognition. saww khēr w giṭṭah baḥar 'do good and throw it in the sea' means: do the good deed, then forget it and don't tell people about it. Recycle the past to play down what you did: ma sawwēt shay, ma ḥabbēt atkallam ʿan il-mawẓūʿ.
grammar: recycle: past tense to play down a good deed; a proverb for recognition
dialogue: A
سيف يقول إنك وديت جارك المستشفى نص الليل
Sēf ygūl innak waddēt jārak il-mustashfa nuṣṣ il-lēl
Sēf says you took your neighbour to hospital in the middle of the night.
B
هيه يا عمي، عياله مسافرين
hē yā ʿammi, ʿyālah msāfrīn
Yes, uncle. His children are away.
A
جزاك الله خير يا ولدي. وشحاله الحين؟
jazāk allāh khēr yā wildi. w shḥālah il-ḥīn?
God reward you, son. And how is he now?
B
وإياك. زين الحمد لله. بس ما سويت شي، أي واحد بيسوي جي
w iyyāk. zēn il-ḥamdu lillāh. bas ma sawwēt shay, ay wāḥid biysawwi chī
And you. He's fine, thank God. But I didn't do anything; anyone would do the same.
A
وليش ما قلت لنا؟ سيف هو اللي قال
w lēsh ma gilt-lana? Sēf huwa illi gāl
So why didn't you tell us? It was Sēf who told us.
B
ما حبيت أتكلم عن الموضوع
ma ḥabbēt atkallam ʿan il-mawẓūʿ
I didn't want to talk about it.
A
زين سويت. سو خير وقطه بحر: يعني سو الزين وانساه، لا تتكلم عنه
zēn sawwēt. saww khēr w giṭṭah baḥar: yaʿni sawwi z-zēn w insāh, la titkallam ʿannah
You did right. 'Do good and throw it in the sea': do the good deed and forget it; don't talk about it.
B
يعني ما أقول لحد؟
yaʿni ma agūl l-ḥad?
So I shouldn't tell anyone?
A
هيه. الأجر عند الله، وهذا يكفي
hē. il-ajr ʿind allāh, w hādha ykaffi
That's right. The reward is with God, and that's enough.
B
صدقت والله. بس سيف من يومه ما يعرف يسكت!
ṣidagt wallāh. bas Sēf min yōmah ma yaʿarf yiskit!
Too true. But Sēf's never been able to keep quiet!
items: do good and throw it in the sea (a proverb)
(recognise) do a good deed, then forget it and don't talk about it; you'll also hear سو خير وقطه بالبحر (bil-baḥar)
you took your neighbour to hospital (to a man)
to a woman: waddēti jārich (وديتي جارج); I took him: waddētah (وديته)
also: ay wāḥid biysawwi chidhi (أي واحد بيسوي جذي)
I didn't want to talk about it
لم أرد أن أتكلم عن الموضوع
don't talk about it (to a man)
to a woman: la titkallamīn ʿannah (لا تتكلمين عنه)
I don't tell anyone, I won't tell anyone
the reward is with God (for a good deed)
he's never been able to keep quiet (lit. since his day)
about a woman: min yōmha ma taʿarf tiskit (من يومها ما تعرف تسكت)
culture: A proverb is a mathal (plural amthāl). Gulf proverbs carry beliefs, habits and morals handed down from older generations. In the next few lessons you'll meet some of them: learn them for recognition, so you know what someone means when they use one.

title: A clever man's mistake
goal: At the office, Maryam tells you that you sent a client the old version of a file; apologise, put it right, and understand her proverb
tip: ghalṭat ish-shāṭir b-alf 'the clever one's mistake counts for a thousand': when someone good at their job slips, it costs more, because others trust their work. Recycle the future b- for putting things right: baṭarrish-lhum 'I'll send them', baʿtadhir 'I'll apologise', bachayyik 'I'll check'.
grammar: recycle: future b- for putting a mistake right; a proverb for recognition
dialogue: A
شفت الإيميل اللي طرشته للعميل الصبح؟
shift il-īmēl illi ṭarrashtah lil-ʿamīl iṣ-ṣubḥ?
Have you seen the email you sent the client this morning?
B
هيه، ليش؟ في شي؟
hē, lēsh? fī shay?
Yes, why? Is something wrong?
A
الملف غلط. طرشت النسخة القديمة، والأرقام كلها قديمة
il-malaff ghalaṭ. ṭarrasht in-nuskha l-gadīma, w il-argām killha gadīma
The file's wrong. You sent the old version, and the figures are all out of date.
B
لا! والله ما انتبهت. آسف، ما أدري شلون صارت
la! wallāh ma ntibaht. āsif, ma adri shlōn ṣārat
Oh no! I honestly didn't notice. Sorry, I don't know how it happened.
A
تصير. بس غلطة الشاطر بألف: العميل يثق في أرقامك
tṣīr. bas ghalṭat ish-shāṭir b-alf: il-ʿamīl yithig fi argāmak
It happens. But a clever man's mistake counts for a thousand: the client trusts your figures.
B
صح. بطرش لهم النسخة الصح الحين، وبعتذر منهم
ṣaḥḥ. baṭarrish-lhum in-nuskha ṣ-ṣaḥḥ il-ḥīn, w baʿtadhir minhum
Right. I'll send them the right version now, and apologise to them.
A
زين. وقول لهم يمسحون الأولى، فيها أغلاط
zēn. w gūl-lhum ymsaḥūn il-ūla, fīha aghlāṭ
Good. And tell them to delete the first one; it's got mistakes in it.
B
إن شاء الله. ومن الحين بشيك كل ملف مرتين
in shāʼ allāh. w min il-ḥīn bachayyik kill malaff marratēn
Will do. And from now on I'll check every file twice.
A
حلو. الكل يغلط، المهم تتعلم منها
ḥilu. il-kill yighlaṭ, il-muhimm titʿallam minha
Good. Everyone makes mistakes; what matters is that you learn from it.
items: the clever one's mistake counts for a thousand (a proverb)
(recognise) when someone good at their job slips, it costs more; said when a capable person makes a mistake
the right version: in-nuskha ṣ-ṣaḥḥ (النسخة الصح)
I didn't notice; you didn't notice (to a man)
to a woman: ma ntibahti (ما انتبهتي)
I don't know how it happened
he trusts your figures (to a man)
(recognise) to a woman: yithig fi argāmich (يثق في أرقامج)
what matters is that you learn from it (to a man)
to a woman: il-muhimm titʿallamīn minha (المهم تتعلمين منها)
task: This week: with a tutor or exchange partner (search a tutoring site for «Emirati Arabic tutor»), ask which Gulf proverbs they still hear at home. Tell them the two you've met (saww khēr w giṭṭah baḥar, ghalṭat ish-shāṭir b-alf), ask whether they know them, and get them to explain one more in Gulf Arabic. Write it down with its meaning.

title: Whoever said 'huh?' heard
goal: At a karak stand, Sēf asks you for a lift to the airport at dawn; try pretending you didn't hear, then agree on your terms
tip: man gāl hā simaʿ 'whoever said huh? heard': said, half joking, to someone who asks 'what?' to dodge a request. Recycle the question word at the end (s4u042): iṭ-ṭayyāra s-sāʿa cham? 'the flight's at what time?' and future b- for the deal: bawaddīk 'I'll take you'.
grammar: recycle: question word at the end; future b- for promises; a proverb for recognition
dialogue: A
يوم الجمعة الفجر عندي طيارة. توديني المطار؟
yōm il-jumʿa l-fajr ʿindi ṭayyāra. twaddīni l-maṭār?
I've got a flight at dawn on Friday. Will you take me to the airport?
B
ها؟ شو قلت؟
hā? shu gilt?
Huh? What did you say?
A
لا تسوي عمرك ما سمعت! من قال ها سمع
la tsawwi ʿumrak ma simaʿt! man gāl hā simaʿ
Don't pretend you didn't hear! Whoever says 'huh?' heard.
B
زين، سمعت. الطيارة الساعة كم؟
zēn, simaʿt. iṭ-ṭayyāra s-sāʿa cham?
OK, I heard. What time's the flight?
A
الساعة ست، يعني لازم نطلع أربع ونص
is-sāʿa sitt, yaʿni lāzim niṭlaʿ arbaʿ w nuṣṣ
At six, so we'll have to leave at half past four.
B
أربع ونص؟! هذا نص الليل يا ريّال!
arbaʿ w nuṣṣ?! hādha nuṣṣ il-lēl yā rayyāl!
Half past four?! That's the middle of the night, man!
A
أدري، وأنا بعد ما أحب أقوم بدري. بس التاكسي غالي
adri, w ana baʿad ma aḥibb agūm badri. bas it-tāksi ghāli
I know; I don't like getting up early either. But a taxi's expensive.
B
خلاص، بوديك. بس الريوق عليك
khalāṣ, bawaddīk. bas ir-riyūg ʿalēk
Fine, I'll take you. But breakfast is on you.
A
تم! وبييب لك شي من السفر بعد
tamm! w bayīb-lak shay min is-safar baʿad
Deal! And I'll bring you something back from the trip, too.
items: whoever says 'huh?' heard (you heard me fine)
(recognise) a proverb, said to someone pretending not to have heard
huh? what did you say? (to a man)
to a woman: hā? shu gilti? (ها؟ شو قلتي؟)
don't pretend you didn't hear (to a man)
to a woman: la tsawwīn ʿumrich ma simaʿti (لا تسوين عمرج ما سمعتي); Kuwait: la tsawwi nafsak (لا تسوي نفسك)
will you take me to the airport? (to a man)
to a woman: the same, twaddīni l-maṭār? (the n of twaddīn drops before -ni)
that's the middle of the night
I don't like getting up early
a taxi's expensive, taxis are expensive
to a woman: ir-riyūg ʿalēch (الريوق عليج)

title: The wolf doesn't trot for nothing
goal: At university, Sēf says a classmate who never talks to you suddenly bought him a karak; work out what he's after
tip: idh-dhīb ma yharwil ʿabath 'the wolf doesn't trot for nothing': when someone who never bothers suddenly makes an effort, he's after something. Recycle guesses with akīd 'must' and the past: akīd yabi shay 'he must want something'; ʿumrah ma kallamni 'he's never spoken to me'.
grammar: recycle: akīd for guesses; ʿumr- ma 'never'; a proverb for recognition
dialogue: A
شفت حمد؟ عزمني على كرك، وسألني عنك!
shift Ḥamad? ʿazamni ʿala karak, w saʼalni ʿannak!
Have you seen Ḥamad? He bought me a karak and asked about you!
B
حمد؟ هذا عمره ما كلمني!
Ḥamad? hādha ʿumrah ma kallamni!
Ḥamad? He's never said a word to me!
A
ولا أنا. الذيب ما يهرول عبث: أكيد يبي شي
wala ana. idh-dhīb ma yharwil ʿabath: akīd yabi shay
Me neither. 'The wolf doesn't trot for nothing': he must want something.
B
شو يبي يعني؟
shu yabi yaʿni?
What would he want, then?
A
باكر آخر يوم حق المشروع، وهو للحين ما بدا
bāchir ākhir yōm ḥagg il-mashrūʿ, w huwa lil-ḥīn ma bada
Tomorrow's the deadline for the project, and he still hasn't started.
B
آها! يعني يبي ملفاتنا
āha! yaʿni yabi malaffātna
Aha! So he wants our files.
A
بالضبط. توه طرش لي: عندكم الملخص؟
biẓ-ẓabṭ. tawwah ṭarrash-li: ʿindkum il-mulakhkhaṣ?
Exactly. He's just texted me: 'Have you got the summary?'
B
قول له يسأل الدكتور. ما بنعطيه شغلنا
gūl-lah yisʼal id-daktōr. ma binʿaṭīh shughulna
Tell him to ask the professor. We're not giving him our work.
A
صح. بس الكرك كان زين!
ṣaḥḥ. bas il-karak kān zēn!
True. But the karak was good!
items: the wolf doesn't trot for nothing (a proverb)
(recognise) when someone like that suddenly makes an effort, he's after something; said of kindness that hides a motive
he treated me to a karak, he bought me a karak
about a woman: akīd tabi shay (أكيد تبي شي)
the last day for the project, the project deadline
I still haven't started: lil-ḥīn ma bdēt (للحين ما بديت)
the summary (of a course or a text)
we won't give him our work

title: A beetle in his mother's eyes
goal: In the car with Sēf, hear what his uncle says about his son Rāshid's football, and understand Sēf's proverb
tip: il-khunfus fi ʿēn ummah ghazāl 'in his mother's eye the beetle is a gazelle': people think the world of what is theirs, above all their own children. Recycle comparatives for 'the best', 'the cleverest': aḥsan lāʿib 'the best player', adhka wāḥid 'the cleverest one'.
grammar: recycle: elatives (aḥsan, adhka) for 'the best'; a proverb for recognition
dialogue: A
عمي بو راشد يقول إن راشد أحسن لاعب في الشارقة!
ʿammi Bū Rāshid ygūl inn Rāshid aḥsan lāʿib fi sh-Shārja!
My uncle Bū Rāshid says Rāshid's the best player in Sharjah!
B
ما شاء الله! شفته يلعب؟
mā shāʼ allāh! shiftah yilʿab?
Mā shāʼ allāh! Have you seen him play?
A
شفته. لاعب عادي، مثله مثل غيره
shiftah. lāʿib ʿādi, mithlah mithil ghērah
I have. He's an ordinary player, no better than anyone else.
B
يمكن عمك يحبه وايد، عشان جي يمدحه
yimkin ʿammak yḥibbah wāyid, ʿashān chī yimdaḥah
Maybe your uncle loves him so much, that's why he praises him.
A
أكيد. الخنفس في عين أمه غزال: كل واحد يشوف عياله أحسن عيال
akīd. il-khunfus fi ʿēn ummah ghazāl: kill wāḥid yshūf ʿyālah aḥsan ʿyāl
Sure. 'In his mother's eye the beetle is a gazelle': everyone thinks their own kids are the best.
B
صح والله. أمي بعد تقول إني أذكى واحد في البيت
ṣaḥḥ wallāh. ummi baʿad tgūl inni adhka wāḥid fi l-bēt
So true. My mum says I'm the cleverest one in the house, too.
A
وانت مصدق؟
w inta mṣaddig?
And you believe it?
B
طبعا! بس إخواني ما يصدقون
ṭabʿan! bas ikhwāni ma yṣaddgūn
Of course! But my brothers don't believe it.
A
زين. وراشد يبي يتعرف عليك، بتشوفه في المجلس الأسبوع الياي
zēn. w Rāshid yabi yitʿarraf ʿalēk, bitshūfah fi l-majlis il-usbūʿ il-yāy
Right. And Rāshid wants to meet you; you'll see him at the majlis next week.
B
إن شاء الله. بس ما بقول له شو قلت!
in shāʼ allāh. bas ma bagūl-lah shu gilt!
I hope so. But I won't tell him what you said!
items: in his mother's eye the beetle is a gazelle (a proverb)
(recognise) people think the world of their own children and things; also with is-sibāl (السبال) 'the monkey' for il-khunfus
no better than anyone else, just like the rest
and you believe it? (to a man)
to a woman: w inti mṣaddga? (وانتي مصدقة؟)
he doesn't believe it: ma yṣaddig (ما يصدق)
he wants to meet you, to get to know you (to a man)
to a woman: yabi yitʿarraf ʿalēch (يبي يتعرف عليج)
culture: The beetle proverb is Emirati, and you'll also hear it with is-sibāl 'the monkey' in place of the beetle. It's said of anything its owner values more than it's worth, and above all of the way parents, especially mothers, see their own children.

title: As the old folk say
goal: In Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Sēf there, he asks about the proverbs you're learning; talk about what they mean
tip: Talk about proverbs: il-amthāl 'proverbs' (one is a mathal, spelt like mithil 'like'), il-mathal fi maḥallah 'the proverb's spot on'. wala + a noun is 'not a single': ma yaʿarf wala mathal 'he doesn't know a single proverb'.
grammar: recycle: wala + noun 'not a single'; baʿaẓ 'some'
dialogue: A
سمعت إنك قاعد تتعلم أمثال، صح؟
simaʿt innak gāʿid titʿallam amthāl, ṣaḥḥ?
I hear you're learning proverbs, is that right?
B
هيه يا عمي. بس بعضها صعب أفهمه
hē yā ʿammi. bas baʿaẓha ṣaʿb afhamah
Yes, uncle. But some of them are hard to understand.
A
عادي يا ولدي. الأمثال كلام ناس أول، وكل مثل وراه حكمة
ʿādi yā wildi. il-amthāl kalām nās awwal, w kill mathal warāh ḥikma
That's normal, son. Proverbs are the words of the old folk, and there's wisdom behind every one.
B
سيف قال مثل عن راشد، بس ما بقول لك شو هو!
Sēf gāl mathal ʿan Rāshid, bas ma bagūl-lak shu huwa!
Sēf said a proverb about Rāshid, but I won't tell you which one!
A
أعرفه! أكيد قال الخنفس في عين أمه غزال. سيف من يومه يمزح
aʿarfah! akīd gāl il-khunfus fi ʿēn ummah ghazāl. Sēf min yōmah yimzaḥ
I know it! He'll have said 'in his mother's eye the beetle is a gazelle'. Sēf's always been a joker.
B
هيه، هو! بس والله ما قصد شي
hē, huwa! bas wallāh ma gaṣad shay
Yes, that's the one! But honestly, he didn't mean anything by it.
A
أدري. والمثل في محله: كلنا نشوف عيالنا أحسن ناس
adri. w il-mathal fi maḥallah: killna nshūf ʿyālna aḥsan nās
I know. And the proverb's spot on: we all think our children are the best.
B
والشباب للحين يقولون أمثال؟
w ish-shabāb lil-ḥīn ygūlūn amthāl?
And do young people still use proverbs?
A
راشد؟ ما يعرف ولا مثل! يقول لي إن هذا كلام شواب
Rāshid? ma yaʿarf wala mathal! ygūl-li inn hādha kalām shuwwāb
Rāshid? He doesn't know a single proverb! He tells me it's old men's talk.
B
زين، أنا بتعلمها بداله!
zēn, ana batʿallamha badālah!
Fine, then I'll learn them for him!
items: one proverb: mathal (مثل), spelt like mithil 'like'
about a feminine noun or plural things: ṣaʿb afhamha (صعب أفهمها)
I didn't mean anything: ma gaṣadt shay (ما قصدت شي)
I won't tell you what it is (to a man)
to a woman: ma bagūl-lich shu huwa (ما بقول لج شو هو)
he doesn't know a single proverb
wala + a noun = not a single: wala kilma (ولا كلمة) 'not a word'
(recognise) ish-shuwwāb = the old men; one old man: shāyib (شايب)
I'll learn them for him, in his place

title: Hala bro! Meeting Rāshid
goal: Outside Bū Rāshid's majlis in Sharjah, with Sēf there, meet his son Rāshid (17), who mixes English into his Arabic
tip: Young people drop English words into Arabic and give them Arabic endings or articles: baṭarrish-lak masij 'I'll send you a message', bil-ʿarabi blīz 'in Arabic, please'. It's fine with friends your age; with elders, stay in Arabic.
grammar: recycle: future b- (baṭarrish-lak); English words inside Arabic
dialogue: A
هلا برو! انت ربيع سيف اللي من لندن؟
hala brō! inta rbīʿ Sēf illi min Landan?
Hey bro! Are you Sēf's friend from London?
B
هلا والله! هيه، أنا. وانت راشد؟
hala wallāh! hē, ana. w inta Rāshid?
Hi there! Yes, that's me. And you're Rāshid?
A
هيه. أبوي ما يسكت عنك، يقول إنك تتكلم عربي زين
hē. ubūy ma yiskit ʿannak, ygūl innak titkallam ʿarabi zēn
Yes. My dad never stops talking about you; he says you speak good Arabic.
B
مشكور. بس انتو تتكلمون وايد سريع!
mashkūr. bas intu titkallamūn wāyid sarīʿ!
Thanks. But you all talk really fast!
A
عادي برو، ونص كلامنا إنقليزي أصلا! سوري، جي نتكلم
ʿādi brō, w nuṣṣ kalāmna ingilīzi aṣlan! sōri, chī nitkallam
No worries, bro, half of what we say is English anyway! Sorry, that's just how we talk.
B
ما عليه. شو تدرس الحين؟
ma ʿalēh. shu tidris il-ḥīn?
That's fine. What are you studying now?
A
آخر سنة في المدرسة، والامتحانات قريبة. والله ضغط!
ākhir sana fi l-madrasa, w il-imtiḥānāt garība. wallāh ẓaghṭ!
It's my last year at school, and the exams are coming up. It's really stressful!
B
الله يوفقك!
allāh ywaffgak!
Good luck!
A
آمين! عطني رقمك، بطرش لك مسج على الواتساب
āmīn! ʿaṭni ragmak, baṭarrish-lak masij ʿala l-wātsāb
Amen! Give me your number; I'll send you a message on WhatsApp.
B
أوكي، بس بالعربي بليز!
ōkē, bas bil-ʿarabi blīz!
OK, but in Arabic, please!
items: hi bro, hey bro (young men's talk)
(recognise) friends only, never to an elder
my dad never stops talking about you (to a man)
أبي لا يكف عن الحديث عنك
(recognise) to a woman: ma yiskit ʿannich (ما يسكت عنج)
you (all) talk really fast (to a group)
to one man: titkallam wāyid sarīʿ (تتكلم وايد سريع); to one woman: titkallamīn wāyid sarīʿ
half of what we say is English
the exams are coming up, are close
I'll send you a message, I'll text you (to a man)
to a woman: baṭarrish-lich masij (بطرش لج مسج); masij is English 'message'
blīz is English 'please': fine with friends your age
culture: Young Emiratis switch between Arabic and English all the time, more with friends and in relaxed settings, less with elders. Bro, OK, sorry and LOL turn up in the middle of Arabic sentences. Keep it for people your own age: with Bū Rāshid and his guests, stay in Arabic.
task: This week: search YouTube for «سوالف شباب» (young people chatting) or «يومياتي» (vlog) with «إماراتي». Within a minute you should hear شو / مب (UAE) or شنو / مو (Kuwait); if not, pick another clip. Write down three sentences where someone drops an English word into Arabic (like masij, ōkē, sōri), then say each aloud twice at the speaker's speed.

title: Kafu! Rāshid's winning goal
goal: Rāshid sends you a voice note: his school team won the final; congratulate him and catch his friends' slang
tip: Young men praise each other with slang you should recognise: kafu! 'well done, you're the man!', rahīb 'awesome', and fashla 'how embarrassing!'. Say your own praise with what you know: mabrūk, tistāhil 'you deserve it'.
grammar: recycle: illi in 'I'm the one who' (ana illi sajjalt); youth slang for recognition
dialogue: A
برو! فزنا بالنهائي، وأنا اللي سجلت الهدف!
brō! fizna bin-nihāʼi, w ana illi sajjalt il-hadaf!
Bro! We won the final, and I'm the one who scored the goal!
B
لا تقول! مبروك يا راشد!
la tgūl! mabrūk yā Rāshid!
No way! Congratulations, Rāshid!
A
الله يبارك فيك! الشباب كلهم يصيحون: كفو يا راشد، كفو!
allāh ybārik fīk! ish-shabāb killhum yṣīḥūn: kafu yā Rāshid, kafu!
Thanks! All the guys were shouting, 'Well done, Rāshid, well done!'
B
تستاهل! وأبوك شو قال؟
tistāhil! w ubūk shu gāl?
You deserve it! And what did your dad say?
A
أبوي قال: رفعت راسي. وصور الهدف عشر مرات، فشلة!
ubūy gāl: rafaʿt rāsi. w ṣawwar il-hadaf ʿashr marrāt, fashla!
My dad said, 'You've made me proud.' And he filmed the goal ten times. So embarrassing!
B
ليش؟ هذا شي حلو! أبوك وايد مستانس
lēsh? hādha shay ḥilu! ubūk wāyid mistānis
Why? That's nice! Your dad's really happy.
A
أدري، بس طرشه في قروب العائلة! حتى سيف شافه
adri, bas ṭarrashah fi grūb il-ʿāyla! ḥatta Sēf shāfah
I know, but he sent it to the family group! Even Sēf's seen it.
B
زين! الحين سيف ما يقدر يقول إنك لاعب عادي
zēn! il-ḥīn Sēf ma yigdar ygūl innak lāʿib ʿādi
Good! Now Sēf can't say you're an ordinary player.
A
قال جي؟! خله يشوف الهدف مرة ثانية، كان رهيب!
gāl chī?! khallah yshūf il-hadaf marra thānya, kān rahīb!
He said that?! Let him watch the goal again; it was awesome!
items: I'm the one who scored the goal
well done! you're the man! (young men's praise)
you've made me proud (to a man; lit. you raised my head)
to a woman: rafaʿti rāsi (رفعتي راسي)

title: Don't just be nice!
goal: On a video call, Rāshid asks you to check his English presentation for school; give him your honest view
tip: Ask for and give an honest opinion: gūl-li ṣ-ṣij 'tell me the truth', la tjāmilni 'don't just say it to be nice', min ṣijji 'I mean it'. Rāshid's la tistahbil! 'stop messing about!' is for friends only: recognise it.
grammar: recycle: imperatives with -li (gūl-li, ṭarrish-li); English verbs with Arabic endings (tchayyik)
dialogue: A
برو، عندي عرض بالإنقليزي باكر. تقدر تشيك عليه؟
brō, ʿindi ʿarẓ bil-ingilīzi bāchir. tigdar tchayyik ʿalēh?
Bro, I've got a presentation in English tomorrow. Can you check it over?
B
أكيد. طرشه لي وبشوفه الليلة
akīd. ṭarrshah-li w bashūfah il-lēla
Sure. Send it over and I'll look at it tonight.
A
طرشته. بس قول لي الصج، لا تجاملني
ṭarrashtah. bas gūl-li ṣ-ṣij, la tjāmilni
Sent. But tell me the truth; don't just be nice.
B
حلو، بس فيه كم غلطة صغيرة
ḥilu, bas fīh cham ghalṭa ṣghīra
It's good, but there are a few small mistakes in it.
A
كم غلطة بس؟ يعني بنجح؟
cham ghalṭa bas? yaʿni banjaḥ?
Only a few? So I'll pass?
B
بتاخذ أعلى درجة في الصف!
bitākhidh aʿla daraja fi ṣ-ṣaff!
You'll get the top mark in the class!
A
لا تستهبل برو، من صجي! المدرس صعب وايد
la tistahbil brō, min ṣijji! il-mudarris ṣaʿb wāyid
Stop messing about, bro, I'm serious! The teacher's really tough.
B
زين، من صجي: صلح الأغلاط اللي حطيت تحتها خط
zēn, min ṣijji: ṣalliḥ il-aghlāṭ illi ḥaṭṭēt taḥt-ha khaṭṭ
OK, seriously: fix the mistakes I've underlined.
A
أوكي! وبتدرب عليه مرتين قبل باكر. ثانكس برو!
ōkē! w batdarrab ʿalēh marratēn gabl bāchir. thānks brō!
OK! And I'll practise it twice before tomorrow. Thanks, bro!
B
العفو. وباكر طرش لي شو صار
il-ʿafu. w bāchir ṭarrish-li shu ṣār
You're welcome. And tomorrow, text me how it went.
items: can you check it over? (to a man)
to a woman: tigdarīn tchayykīn ʿalēh? (تقدرين تشيكين عليه؟)
tell me the truth (to a man)
to a woman: gūlī-li ṣ-ṣij (قولي لي الصج)
don't just say it to be nice, don't flatter me (to a man)
to a woman: la tjāmlīni (لا تجامليني)
the top mark, the highest grade
stop messing about! don't act daft! (friends only) (to a man)
(recognise) to a woman: la tistahblīn (لا تستهبلين)
are you serious? min ṣijjak? (من صجك؟) to a man
I underlined them (lit. I put a line under them)

title: A desert trip with the gang
goal: Rāshid invites you to a weekend desert trip with his friends; ask where, who's going and what to bring
tip: Plans for the weekend use future b-: biniṭlaʿ kashta 'we're going on a desert trip', binishwi 'we'll grill', huwa illi biysūg 'he's the one driving'. Rāshid mixes in English (il-wīkind, ōkē); his ish-shilla 'the gang' and wanāsa 'great fun' are for recognition.
grammar: recycle: future b- for weekend plans; illi biy- 'the one who will'
dialogue: A
برو، الويكند بنطلع كشتة ويا الشلة. تيي ويانا؟
brō, il-wīkind biniṭlaʿ kashta wiyya sh-shilla. tiyi wiyyāna?
Bro, at the weekend we're going on a desert trip with the gang. Will you come with us?
B
كشتة؟ وين بالضبط؟
kashta? wēn biẓ-ẓabṭ?
A desert trip? Where exactly?
A
في البر، ورا مليحة. بنشوي وبنسولف للصبح، وناسة!
fi l-barr, warā Mlēḥa. binishwi w binsōlif liṣ-ṣubḥ, wanāsa!
Out in the desert, past Mleiha. We'll barbecue and chat till morning: great fun!
B
حلو! بس سيف بيروح بعد؟
ḥilu! bas Sēf biyrūḥ baʿad?
Nice! But is Sēf going too?
A
أكيد، هو اللي بيسوق. وانت ييب الفحم، أوكي؟
akīd, huwa illi biysūg. w inta yīb il-faḥam, ōkē?
Of course; he's the one driving. And you bring the charcoal, OK?
B
تم. ولازم ألبس شي معين؟
tamm. w lāzim albas shay mʿayyan?
Done. And do I have to wear anything in particular?
A
لا، عادي. بس لا تيي بكندورة بيضا، بتتوسخ!
la, ʿādi. bas la tiyi b-kandūra bēẓa, bititwassakh!
No, anything. Just don't come in a white kandura; it'll get dirty!
B
زين. وانتو كل ويكند تطلعون؟
zēn. w intu kill wīkind tiṭlaʿūn?
OK. And do you lot go out every weekend?
A
إذا ما عندنا امتحانات. بس هالمرة أكيد بنطلع!
idha ma ʿindana imtiḥānāt. bas hal-marra akīd biniṭlaʿ!
When we haven't got exams. But this time we're definitely going!
items: we're going on a desert trip, an outing
(recognise) a kashta (كشتة) is a trip out to the desert or the countryside with friends or family
the gang, my group of friends
we'll grill, we'll have a barbecue
she's the one driving: hiya illi bitsūg (هي اللي بتسوق)
to a woman: yībi l-faḥam (ييبي الفحم)

title: Arabic with Grandma, English with the gang
goal: Driving back with Rāshid, ask why he spoke no English in the majlis, and when he uses which language
tip: Say what goes with whom using wiyya 'with' and w bas 'only': wiyya yaddti ʿarabi w bas 'with my grandma, Arabic only'. Recycle wala + noun: ma gilt wala kilma 'I didn't say a single word'.
dialogue: A
شفت؟ في المجلس ما قلت ولا كلمة إنقليزي
shift? fi l-majlis ma gilt wala kilma ingilīzi
See? In the majlis I didn't say a single word of English.
B
هيه، لاحظت. ليش؟
hē, lāḥaẓt. lēsh?
Yes, I noticed. Why?
A
ويا أبوي ويدتي عربي وبس. الإنقليزي ويا الشلة
wiyya ubūy w yaddti ʿarabi w bas. il-ingilīzi wiyya sh-shilla
With my dad and my grandma it's Arabic only. English is for the gang.
B
بس ليش تتكلمون إنقليزي أصلا؟
bas lēsh titkallamūn ingilīzi aṣlan?
But why do you speak English at all?
A
ما أدري، طبيعي عندنا. في أشيا أسهل أقولها بالإنقليزي
ma adri, ṭabīʿi ʿindana. fī ashya ashal agūlha bil-ingilīzi
I don't know, it's normal for us. Some things are easier to say in English.
B
وأي أشيا أسهل بالعربي؟
w ay ashya ashal bil-ʿarabi?
And which things are easier in Arabic?
A
الدعا، والسوالف ويا الأهل، والمزح بعد!
id-duʿa, w is-sawālif wiyya l-ahal, w il-mazḥ baʿad!
Prayers, chatting with the family, and joking too!
B
وفي الواتساب؟ تكتب عربي؟
w fi l-wātsāb? tiktib ʿarabi?
And on WhatsApp? Do you write in Arabic?
A
عربي بحروف إنقليزية، وأرقام بدال بعض الحروف. بعلمك!
ʿarabi b-ḥurūf ingilīziyya, w argām badāl baʿaẓ il-ḥurūf. baʿallmak!
Arabic in English letters, with numbers instead of some letters. I'll teach you!
B
لا شكرا، الحروف العربية تكفيني!
la shukran, il-ḥurūf il-ʿarabiyya tkaffīni!
No thanks, Arabic letters are enough for me!
items: not a single word of English
I noticed; you noticed (to a man)
(recognise) Arabic typed this way, with numbers for some letters, is called Arabeezy (عربيزي)
the Arabic letters, the Arabic alphabet
culture: Young Emiratis say they switch on purpose, not at random: some ideas come out more easily in English, others in Arabic. English is everywhere at university and work, but Arabic is how they talk to grandparents, pray and keep their ties to their heritage. Online, many type Arabic in English letters and numbers, which they call Arabeezy.

title: Don't call my dad bro!
goal: At the majlis door, Rāshid tells you which of his words you mustn't use with his father and the older guests
tip: Match the word to the listener: brō and ōkē with friends your age; yā ʿammi and ṭāl ʿumrak with elders. Recycle Form VII for what can't be said: ma tingāl 'it isn't said, you don't say it' (a feminine noun, here a word: kilma).
grammar: recycle: Form VII ma tingāl; register and address
dialogue: A
يلا، أبوي داخل ويا الضيوف. بس لا تقول له برو!
yalla, ubūy dākhil wiyya ẓ-ẓyūf. bas la tgūl-lah brō!
Come on, my dad's inside with the guests. Just don't call him bro!
B
لا تخاف! أدري، أقول له يا عمي
la tkhāf! adri, agūl-lah yā ʿammi
Don't worry! I know: I call him yā ʿammi.
A
زين. والضيوف الكبار، قول لهم طال عمرك
zēn. w iẓ-ẓyūf il-kbār, gūl-lhum ṭāl ʿumrak
Good. And to the older guests, say ṭāl ʿumrak.
B
وسوري وأوكي؟ ما تنقال بعد؟
w sōri w ōkē? ma tingāl baʿad?
And 'sorry' and 'OK'? Can't you say those either?
A
تنقال، عادي. بس قدام الشواب خلك على العربي
tingāl, ʿādi. bas jiddām ish-shuwwāb khallak ʿala l-ʿarabi
You can say them, that's fine. But in front of the old men, stick to Arabic.
B
وانت؟ ما تقول برو قدام أبوك؟
w inta? ma tgūl brō jiddām ubūk?
And you? Don't you say bro in front of your dad?
A
أبد! مرة قلتها بالغلط، وأبوي طالعني جي…
abad! marra giltha bil-ghalaṭ, w ubūy ṭālaʿni chī…
Never! Once I said it by mistake, and my dad gave me this look…
B
وبعدين؟ شو صار؟
w baʿdēn? shu ṣār?
And then? What happened?
A
قال: هذا مجلس، مب ملعب! ومن ذاك اليوم ما قلتها
gāl: hādha majlis, mub malʿab! w min dhāk il-yōm ma giltha
He said, 'This is a majlis, not a football pitch!' And I haven't said it since that day.
B
خلاص، فهمت. يلا ندخل!
khalāṣ, fhimt. yalla nidkhil!
Right, got it. Let's go in!
items: don't call him bro (to a man)
to a woman: la tgūlīn-lah brō (لا تقولين له برو)
one older guest: iẓ-ẓēf il-kbīr (الضيف الكبير)
it isn't said, you don't say it (of a word)
of a masculine noun: ma yingāl (ما ينقال)
in front of the old men
to a woman: khallich ʿala l-ʿarabi (خلج على العربي)
he gave me this look (lit. he looked at me like this)
this is a majlis, not a football pitch
task: This week: record two short voice notes saying you can't come on Friday and suggesting another day. Send the first to Rāshid: casual, with a few English words (brō, sōri, ōkē). Then say the same thing to Bū Rāshid: yā ʿammi or ṭāl ʿumrak, all in Arabic, no English. Listen back and check that the two really sound different.

title: Checkpoint 4.7: back in the majlis
goal: Checkpoint: in Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Sēf and Rāshid there, play down how you helped Rāshid, and keep your English out of it
tip: Review, and now you say it: ma ḥabbēt atkallam ʿan il-mawẓūʿ, tistāhil, min ṣijji, ma tingāl, khallak ʿala l-ʿarabi, and the proverbs you recognise in Bū Rāshid's lines. Here, in front of an elder, B's Arabic has no English in it.
grammar: checkpoint 4.7 (s4u084–s4u095): proverbs for recognition, youth speech and register
dialogue: A
راشد يقول إنك ساعدته في العرض حق المدرسة
Rāshid ygūl innak sāʿadtah fi l-ʿarẓ ḥagg il-madrasa
Rāshid says you helped him with his school presentation.
B
شي بسيط يا عمي. هو اللي اشتغل عليه
shay basīṭ yā ʿammi. huwa illi ishtaghal ʿalēh
It was nothing, uncle. He's the one who worked on it.
A
والمدرس قال إنه أحسن عرض في الصف. رفع راسي!
w il-mudarris gāl innah aḥsan ʿarẓ fi ṣ-ṣaff. rafaʿ rāsi!
And the teacher said it was the best presentation in the class. He's made me proud!
B
يستاهل! تدرب عليه وايد
yistāhil! tdarrab ʿalēh wāyid
He deserves it! He practised it a lot.
A
وانت ما قلت لنا شي! سو خير وقطه بحر، ها؟
w inta ma gilt-lana shay! saww khēr w giṭṭah baḥar, hā?
And you didn't tell us a thing! 'Do good and throw it in the sea', eh?
B
لا والله، بس ما حبيت أتكلم عن الموضوع
la wallāh, bas ma ḥabbēt atkallam ʿan il-mawẓūʿ
No, really, I just didn't want to talk about it.
A
وسيف يقول إنك صرت تقول برو وأوكي!
w Sēf ygūl innak ṣirt tgūl brō w ōkē!
And Sēf says you've started saying bro and OK!
B
بس ويا راشد! هني عربي وبس
bas wiyya Rāshid! hni ʿarabi w bas
Only with Rāshid! In here it's Arabic only.
A
زين تسوي. ولا تقول لي برو، ترا ما أرد عليك!
zēn tsawwi. w la tgūl-li brō, tara ma arudd ʿalēk!
Good for you. And don't you call me bro, or I won't answer you!
B
أبد يا عمي! من صجي، ما تنقال هني
abad yā ʿammi! min ṣijji, ma tingāl hni
Never, uncle! Honestly, it's not a word for in here.
items: it was nothing, just a small thing
he's the one who worked on it
she's the one who worked on it: hiya illi ishtaghalat ʿalēh (هي اللي اشتغلت عليه)
the best presentation in the class
I practised it: tdarrabt ʿalēh (تدربت عليه)
good for you, you're doing the right thing (to a man)
to a woman: zēn tsawwīn (زين تسوين)
I won't answer you (to a man)
to a woman: ma arudd ʿalēch (ما أرد عليج)
